title: Open covers and compactness
terms: covering; open cover; finite subcover; compact space; finite intersection property; sequen- tial compactness.

exposition.text:
A space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. To disprove compactness, produce
one open cover for which no finite selection suffices. Finite spaces and indiscrete spaces are
compact; an infinite discrete space fails because the cover by singletons has no finite subcover.
Closed subsets of compact spaces are compact, and products of finitely many compact spaces
are compact. In metric spaces compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness, meaning
every sequence has a convergent subsequence with its limit in the space. This equivalence is not
a definition valid for all topological spaces.
An open cover is a family of open sets whose union contains the space or subset being covered;
a finite subcover selects finitely many members of that same family. A family has the finite
intersection property when every finite subfamily has nonempty intersection. For closed sub-
sets of a compact space this property guarantees a nonempty full intersection; the nested-set
question is a special case.

question.text:
An infinite subset of a compact metric space must have
(A) A finite number of points
(B) A limit point in the space
(C) A limit point belonging to the subset
(D) Nonempty interior
(E) Positive diameter bounded below by one

solution.text:
Compact metric spaces are limit-point compact. The limit point may lie outside the subset,
as zero does for {1/n : n ≥ 1} ⊂ [0, 1].

question.text:
Let X, Y be compact spaces and f : X → R, g : Y → R continuous. Which property must the
set C = {(x, y) ∈ X × Y : f (x) = g(y)} have?
(A) It is nonempty. (B) It is open in X × Y .
(C) It is connected. (D) It is finite.
(E) It is compact.

solution.text:
The finite product X × Y is compact. The function (x, y) 7→ f(x) − g(y) is continuous, so C
is the inverse image of the closed set {0} and is closed in the product. A closed subset of a
compact space is compact, even when the spaces are not Hausdorff. No overlap of the two
ranges was assumed, so C may be empty.

question.text:
In an arbitrary topological space, a sequence x converges to x. Which property must K =
n
{x} ∪ {x : n ≥ 1} have, with its subspace topology?
n
(A) It is finite.
(B) It is compact.
(C) It is Hausdorff.
(D) Every subset of K is closed.
(E) It is connected.

solution.text:
Given an open cover of K, select a member containing x. By convergence it contains all
but finitely many of the terms x . Choose one cover member for each remaining point;
n
together these form a finite subcover. This argument uses the cover definition and holds
without Euclidean boundedness or a Hausdorff assumption. A convergent reciprocal se-
quence with its limit need not be connected.
